issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Never alone with another person' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The triggers, threat items, and memory content suggest a combat/military trauma pattern centered on environmental danger cues (fire, silence, shouting, sensory flashback phenomena), not an interpersonal danger pattern specifically involving being alone with another person. This strategy therefore appears to address a different trauma context than the one represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Feeling dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is more typically linked to sexual or severe interpersonal violation trauma. In this profile, the surrounding triggers, memory, and threat items point to a military combat-type danger formulation rather than contamination-based shame. Paired with the 'never alone with another person' strategy, it pulls the profile toward a different trauma meaning structure that is not otherwise represented.

vignette:
Mariana is a fifty-four-year-old combat engineer who spent twenty-two years in the United States Army, much of that time deployed to active combat zones. She is married to a retired mechanic, and they live in a quiet suburban neighborhood outside of San Antonio. She came to therapy at her husband's urging, though she was not sure what talking could possibly change. Her PCL-5 score of 62 reflected the severity of what she had been carrying for nearly a decade.

The event that fractured her life happened during her third deployment, in a forward operating base in eastern Afghanistan. A routine route-clearing patrol had been called back early, and Mariana was in the motor pool inspecting a damaged MRAP when an improvised explosive device detonated near the perimeter. The blast wave threw her against a fuel truck. She remembers the heat-a specific, searing temperature on her skin, as though the air itself had turned solid and burning. She remembers the fire that erupted from the vehicle next to her, flames climbing the side of a supply tent, and the shouting-men screaming orders, names, warnings, all blending into a roaring chaos. She cannot tell a clear story of what happened after that, not even to herself. The minutes are a smear of noise and heat and the smell of diesel. She knows she helped pull two soldiers to cover. She knows she was later told she had a concussion and second-degree burns on her forearms. But the sequence, the logic of cause and effect, the narrative she could tell another person-that never formed.

In the years since, Mariana has learned to live inside a body that feels constantly tense, braced for something. She scans every environment she enters, her eyes moving from corners to doorways to windows before she can stop them. At the grocery store, she notices the exits. At a restaurant, she positions herself with her back to the wall. She has come to believe that the world is a dangerous place, and that this vigilance is the only thing keeping her safe. Unusual silence terrifies her-a quiet house, a pause in conversation, the absence of traffic noise on a Sunday morning-because silence, in her experience, is what comes before the blast. She has difficulty concentrating on anything that requires sustained attention. She will be reading a manual or watching a television show and suddenly she is back in the heat, hearing the shouting in her head, the exact pitch and urgency of those voices, and she has no idea how much time has passed.

She has developed a pervasive strategy of avoiding anything that could be stressful. This has narrowed her life considerably. She stopped attending family gatherings because someone might ask about her service. She stopped driving past the VFW hall. She stopped watching news coverage of military operations, then stopped watching news altogether. She told herself she was protecting her peace. But the cost has been concrete. Her husband has taken over all household responsibilities that involve leaving the house, because Mariana cannot tolerate the unpredictability of errands. He handles the bills, the shopping, the appointments. She has not visited her adult daughter in three years. She has not had a conversation with a friend that lasted more than ten minutes. She numbs her feelings because when she lets herself feel anything, what rises first is a cold, grinding sense of injustice-that what happened to her was deeply unfair, and that nothing has been done about it. She does not know who she would hold accountable, or what reparation would look like. She only knows that something is wrong with her as a person, that she is broken in a way that cannot be fixed, and that the rest of the world goes on living while she stays frozen in that moment of heat and noise.

What finally brought her to seek help was not her own distress but a single moment of terror. Her husband was grilling in the backyard, and a gust of wind made the flames flare. Mariana saw the fire, felt the remembered temperature on her skin, and before she knew what she was doing, she had grabbed a garden hose and sprayed the grill until it was dead. Her husband stood there, stunned, and said nothing. Later that night, he told her quietly that he could not watch her live like this anymore. She is afraid of what will happen if she lets the memories come fully, afraid that she will fall apart and never put herself back together. But she is also tired. She is tired of the scanning, the tension, the silence that feels like a threat. She came to therapy because she does not know what else to do, and because she cannot bear the thought of losing the one person who has stayed.
